title: service-path-mapping-and-tls-termination-patterns
content:
Purpose:
This note captures heuristics and proposed patterns for mapping service-level paths to network routing and where TLS termination should occur across our multi-region fabric. It is intended to help platform teams decide between edge termination, mesh-sidecar termination, and SNI passthrough for different workloads, and to record control-plane considerations for failover and policy enforcement.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments where we control the control plane and data plane.
- Primary traffic types: API inference (low-latency, short-lived), streaming websocket/chat (long-lived), control-plane gRPC (internal), and telemetry/export (batch/stream).
- Regions: us-west, us-east, eu-central, ap-southeast.
- We run an envoy-based service mesh in most clusters but allow sidecarless paths for latency-sensitive unary RPCs.

Design goals / constraints:
- Minimize extra hops for low-latency inference requests while preserving zero-trust identity and observability.
- Allow predictable failover across regions under degraded control-plane connectivity.
- Keep operational complexity reasonable — patterns should be composable and debuggable without deep platform expertise.
- Provide clear audit points for egress (billing, policy, external compliance).

Pattern catalog (recommendations):
1) Edge TLS termination + mTLS to mesh (recommended for general public API traffic)
   - Flow: CDN/TCP LB (TLS offload) -> Edge Gateway (authz, rate-limit, RBAC) -> mTLS into mesh sidecars -> service.
   - Rationale: offloading TLS at the CDN/edge reduces CPU on nodes and allows WAF/rate-limits close to the origin. mTLS inside the cluster preserves service-to-service identity and simplifies policy enforcement.
   - Pros: strong audit point at edge; simple certificate lifecycle at control-plane; good observability.
   - Cons: double-termination increases surface area for TLS misconfiguration; must ensure end-to-end identity mapping (X-Forwarded-Client-Cert or SAN forwarding).
   - When to use: public APIs, multi-tenant endpoints where tenant-level auth and rate-limiting happen at the edge.

2) SNI passthrough -> sidecar/host termination (for strict E2E cert requirements)
   - Flow: CDN/TCP LB (SNI passthrough) -> node-level listener -> service-side TLS termination (sidecar or in-process).
   - Rationale: preserves end-to-end cert visibility for customers that require their cert presented to services (private deployments, regulated customers).
   - Pros: real E2E TLS without interception; suitable for customer-managed certs/HSM-backed keys.
   - Cons: limited L7 visibility at edge; harder to do global routing decisions based on application-level headers.
   - When to use: private deployments with compliance constraints or bring-your-own-certs scenarios.

3) Edge TLS passthrough + mesh L7 inspection only for internal services (hybrid)
   - Flow: CDN/TCP LB (SNI passthrough) -> edge node that does minimal routing -> mesh sidecar performs L7 inspection for internal services only, leaving other traffic untouched.
   - Use-case: mixed tenancy where some customers require E2E TLS and others rely on platform features (retry, observability).

4) Sidecarless L7 termination for ultra-low-latency unary inference calls
   - Flow: CDN/LB -> LB performs auth & routing -> direct in-process TLS termination in serving runtime (no envoys).
   - Rationale: reduce latency and tail variance from sidecar processing and extra socket hops.
   - Important safeguards: mandatory request-level auth tokens validated by the process, enforced telemetry hooks, and a control-plane policy that only allows sidecarless mode for designated pod selectors and machine types.

Egress topology patterns and policy enforcement:
- Egress exit points must be limited and tagged by region and cost-center. Use a regional egress-proxy fleet (small set of well-instrumented VM pools) for outbound traffic to internet services (telemetry, S3, external model registries).
- Policy: all egress must be declared in a service-level egress manifest. An admission webhook rejects pods that attempt to open arbitrary external IPs.
- NAT vs Proxy: prefer proxy-based egress (explicit HTTP CONNECT/HTTPS) where possible for visibility and per-tenant auditing. Use SNAT at node-level only for legacy tooling that cannot be proxied.
- Cost accounting: inject an egress-tagging header at the proxy that includes org_id, project, and route_id so downstream billing systems can attribute bytes.

Control plane routing and failover considerations:
- Control-plane partition tolerance: do not assume global control-plane availability for data-plane routing. Data plane should continue serving with cached config for 5–30 minutes based on policy category (routing-critical vs policy-light).
- Config sync: use incremental deltas and versioned route manifests. Each data-plane node stores a small history of route versions; in failover we switch to the last-known-good route (deterministic).
- Failover modes:
   * Prefer-local: route stays within same region if healthy (default).
   * Cross-region-failover: only for routes tagged as geo-failover-enabled. This avoids unexpected cost spikes.
   * Best-effort-global: used for admin/control-plane only.
- Sticky-session policies: avoid long-lived node-affinity unless application requires it. For streaming/chat, use a resilience token in the initial handshake that allows reattachment without session loss.

Service Mesh interactions and policy placement:
- Split responsibility: mesh enforces service-to-service auth and telemetry; edge gateways enforce tenant-level quotas, ingress ACLs, and DDoS protections.
- Policy overlap rules: edge > mesh > in-app. If a rule conflict arises, the highest precedence aborts the request and emits an event to the routing-audit log.
- Sidecar resource budgeting: cap envoy CPU for p99-sensitive pods and provide a sidecarless escape hatch described above. Use runtime flags to enable/disable sidecars for a given namespace by default.

Observability & debugging patterns:
- Trace headers: ensure trace-id is preserved across TLS termination boundaries; when double-termination is used, re-attach trace context at the edge and mark the boundary.
- Route provenance: every request should carry a route-id (uuid) that maps to the route manifest version; expose a route lookup endpoint in the control-plane that accepts route-id and returns resolution history for that request.
- Synthetic canary flows: deploy short-lived canary routes that exercise cross-region routing logic after any control-plane rollout; automate smoke checks for latency and error rates.

Operational playbook snippets (quick wins):
- For new public endpoints, default to Edge TLS termination + mTLS inside cluster. Only enable SNI passthrough after customer signoff.
- Add egress-manifest validation to CI: every PR that introduces a new external host needs a JIRA ticket and an egress entry.
- Run weekly job that detects nodes serving sidecarless routes and verifies telemetry is present.

Open questions / trade-offs to decide:
- Should we mandate proxy-based egress in private deployments where customers manage their own NAT? (security/audit vs ops friction)
- Do we require client cert CCA mapping for tenant identity propagation, or rely on JWT-based mapping at the edge?
- Acceptable duration for cached route-only operation when control-plane is unreachable (15 min vs 60 min).

Next steps and action items:
- (Avery) Draft PR updating the route manifest schema to include route-id and geo-failover flag. Related: PR #512 in serving-runtime.
- (Priya) Prototype edge->mesh identity propagation using XFCC header standardized format.
- (Miguel + SRE) Run chaos tests that simulate control-plane latency and validate data-plane cached config behavior (JIRA-INFRA-3421).
- (Lena) Add egress header tagging into regional egress-proxy and expose ingestion for billing pipeline.

References and links:
- Confluence: Service Mesh Routing Patterns (linked_artifacts above)
- Jira: JIRA-INFRA-3421 (control-plane resilience tests)
- Repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime (see PRs for route schema)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working doc; expect iterative changes. Please comment with actual corner cases you've seen in Dedicated/Private customers where SNI passthrough was required.
